questions.q: What makes a 'silent' model-quality degradation hard to detect compared to a typical service outage?
options: It only happens during scheduled maintenance windows
Standard infrastructure metrics like availability and latency can stay fully healthy while the model's decisions quietly get worse
It always coincides with a latency spike
It always triggers the error-budget page immediately
questions.explain: Silent degradation is exactly the case where the service's SLOs (availability, latency, even freshness) all look green, so nothing pages — a human or a business-side metric notices first.

questions.q: In the lesson's scenario, why does checking feature freshness alone fail to catch the problem?
options: The feature was arriving on time (fresh) but its underlying distribution had shifted, so freshness being fine didn't mean the feature was still correct
Freshness checks were turned off entirely
The fraud team never reported the issue
Freshness only applies to model versions, not features
questions.explain: A feature can be perfectly fresh and still wrong if whatever produces it upstream changes — freshness measures timing, not correctness of the values themselves.

questions.q: What does a Population Stability Index (PSI) score above roughly 0.2 indicate?
options: The on-call engineer has missed a page
The error budget has been fully exhausted
A significant shift between the training-time distribution and the current production distribution of a feature, likely explaining degraded model behavior
The model has not been retrained recently
questions.explain: A PSI score at or above about 0.2 is the standard threshold indicating a significant population shift that typically warrants action, such as investigating or retraining.

questions.q: Why is retraining the model NOT listed as an immediate incident-mitigation action in this lesson?
options: Retraining would violate the model registry's versioning rules
Retraining takes time and needs clean data, so it belongs in a deliberate retraining pipeline run after the incident, not as a scramble during it
Retraining is never appropriate for a degraded model
Retraining is only possible before a model is first deployed
questions.explain: Mitigation needs to stop the damage quickly — a killswitch, rollback, or fallback rule — while retraining is a slower, deliberate action for after the incident is stable.

questions.q: What is the defining feature of a blameless postmortem, as described in the Google SRE book's postmortem culture chapter?
options: It identifies which specific individual caused the incident so they can be retrained
It is optional once the incident is mitigated
It skips the timeline and focuses only on the fix
It identifies contributing causes without indicting any individual or team, assuming everyone acted reasonably given what they could see
questions.explain: A blameless postmortem focuses on systemic contributing causes rather than individual fault, which keeps people willing to report and investigate issues honestly.
